secretGenerated: A client secret was generated and is in the oauthClientSecret box below. Nothing has been written: it becomes this application's credential when you create it. Its token endpoint authentication method is set to client_secret_basic where none was chosen, and the token endpoint accepts the secret either in an Authorization: Basic header (client_secret_basic) or as a client_secret form parameter (client_secret_post).
filled: Filled in with the invented person for {username}. Nobody has been created. Edit or clear anything you like and press Create the user.
appPassword.heading: The app password "{name}" for {who}, shown once
appPassword.warn: Note it now. This service stores a scrypt hash and cannot show it again. Give it to {who} by a channel you trust. It is accepted at {doors} only — never at the sign-in screen.
appPassword.caep: A CAEP credential-change (password, create) went to every stream that asked for it and covers this person.
reset.passwordHeading: The new password for {who}, shown once
reset.passwordWarn: Note it now. This service stores a scrypt hash and cannot show it again — not this console, not /admin-api.
reset.forced: It works ONCE, at the sign-in screen, where {who} is made to choose their own before anything is signed in.
reset.notForced: The forced change could not be recorded, so it will go on working until somebody changes it.
reset.linkHeading: The password reset link for {who}, shown once
reset.linkWarn: Send it to {who} by a channel you trust. Valid until {until}. Anybody holding it can set this person's password, so treat it as the credential it is. It is spent when the new password is stored, not when it is opened.
reset.revoked: Their old password was REMOVED, so until the link is used they cannot sign in with a password.
reset.noPassword: They had no password to remove.
reset.signals: Shared Signals: a CAEP credential-change and a RISC account-credential-change-required went to every stream that asked for those types and covers this person, and each session the sign-out ended sent its own CAEP session-revoked.
created.passwordWarn: This is the only time this value exists anywhere but in the hash on the entry. Copy it now and send it to {username} by whatever channel you already use. Nothing in this service can show it again — not this console, not /admin-api, not an ldapsearch, which sees a scrypt hash. If it is lost, set a new one; there is no recovery because there is nothing to recover.
created.mailed: It went to {to}, valid until {until}, and is not shown here. Monitoring →
created.linkWarn: Valid until {until}, and shown once. This service stores only a hash of the token in it and cannot produce the link again — issuing another invalidates this one, which is also how a link that never arrived is replaced. Treat it as the credential it is: anybody holding it can finish setting up this account, choosing a password or enrolling a security key. It is spent when that setup FINISHES rather than when the link is opened, so a mail scanner or a browser prefetch cannot burn it. There is deliberately no self-service version of this link: until the account is activated nobody has proved the address on it is theirs. Tick mail the activation link on the form to have this service send it instead.
created.hashSet: set — a scrypt hash, not shown here
created.entry: The entry exactly as the store holds it, which is what an ldapsearch under this realm's base DN returns. Attribute names are lower-cased because LDAP attribute descriptions are case-insensitive and this store normalises them on the way in. The two attributes that hold a verifier are named rather than printed;
created.remember: . Remember that they will not appear in the Users TABLE until they authenticate: that list is who this service has SEEN.
realm.heading: The "{realm}" realm's administrator, shown once
realm.warn: Note it now. It is stored as a scrypt hash and cannot be shown again. It works once, at that realm's sign-in screen, where a new password must be chosen. This account administers the "{realm}" realm and nothing else.
keytab.once: This keytab is shown once. It is not kept in the clear anywhere and this service cannot show it again;
keytab.oncePerson: another is made by resetting the password again, or by the person from their own password on the portal.
keytab.onceService: a lost keytab is replaced by rotating, which makes a new key.
keytab.changed: {username}'s password was changed to {how, select, generated {a generated one that nobody was shown, so this keytab is the only thing that signs them in until a password is set again} other {the one you typed}}, and they were signed out of everything.
keytab.versionsText: {kvnos} — the previous version stays in it, as after ktadd, for tickets already issued under it
keytab.terminal: Or, in a terminal: base64 -d > {file} and paste the text below, then klist -k -e {file} to see the entries.
eab.warn: Copy the HMAC key now. It is stored sealed on the entry and is never shown again.
scep.warn: The challenge password for {uri} ({profile}). It is shown once and cannot be shown again.
did.warn: This is the only time the private key is shown. This service keeps it sealed, to sign the application’s Domain Linkage Credentials, and shows it on no page after this one. If your copy is lost, generate another with replace ticked.
did.how: Sign as the DID with this key and name the verification method above as the kid; a verifier resolves the DID and finds the public key in the document.
tls.warn: This is the only time these files can be downloaded. The private key is not kept by this service — not on the application’s entry, not in the certificate register — and nothing on this console or on /admin-api hands it out again. If it is lost, revoke the certificate and issue another.
tls.how: How the application uses it. Present it on the TLS connection to the token endpoint with client_id={client} and a token_endpoint_auth_method of tls_client_auth on the entry: RFC 8705 section 2.1 authenticates it because this realm issued it to this application, with nothing else registered. Every access token issued on that connection carries cnf["x5t#S256"] of this certificate (section 3), so the application presents the same certificate to the resource servers. curl --cert {chain} --key {key} --pass <file password> -d grant_type=client_credentials -d client_id={client} <base>/oauth2/token
pep.warn: This is the only time this service will show you this key. It is not on the PEP’s entry and nothing in this console or in /admin-api opens it again. Save it as the file PEP_HTTPS_KEY names.
pep.chain: The certificate followed by its chain (the Issuing CA and this realm’s Intermediate) — the file PEP_HTTPS_CERT names:
pep.anchor: The anchor a client of that listener installs — this service’s Root CA, which the chain deliberately leaves out:
person.warn: This is the only time this service will show you this key. It is sealed on {person}’s entry as {attribute} and nothing in this console or in /admin-api opens it again. Copy it now; issuing again replaces it.
person.saml: The assertion it signs carries an <Issuer> and a <Subject> of {issuer}, an <AudienceRestriction> naming this service’s token endpoint, a bearer <SubjectConfirmation>, a NotOnOrAfter and an ID, is signed with an XML Signature over the <Assertion>, and is presented as grant_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:saml2-bearer with assertion=<base64url>. The certificate’s thumbprint is {thumbprint}.
person.jwt: The assertion it signs carries iss and sub of {issuer}, an aud of this service’s token endpoint or issuer, an exp and a jti, and is presented as grant_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:jwt-bearer with assertion=<the JWT>. kid is {kid} and the algorithm is {alg}.
person.certificate: The certificate, which is public and is also on the entry:
